Let $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-integers]]) with $b > 0$. Then there exist
integers $q$ and $r$ with

$$a \;=\; qb + r, \qquad 0 \le r < b,$$

and the pair $(q,r)$ with these two properties is unique.

We say $b$ **divides** $a$, written $b \mid a$, when $a = qb$ for some
$q \in \mathbb{Z}$; by the above, for $b > 0$ this holds exactly when the
remainder $r$ is $0$.

The set of **natural numbers** is the **smallest inductive set**
([[def-inductive-set]]),

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]] (the
Axiom of Infinity, [[def-axiom-of-infinity]], supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of von Neumann naturals
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ is itself the set of its predecessors,
the order being the additive order of [[def-nat-order]] identified with
membership in [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists ([[def-equinumerous]],
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). A set $A$ is **finite** when
$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable]]).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

**(d) Equality of cardinalities is equinumerosity.** For finite $A$ and $B$:
$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

Let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets and write

$$A^{B} := \{\, f : f \text{ is a function } B \to A \,\}.$$

Then $A^{B}$ is finite and $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = \lvert A\rvert^{\lvert B\rvert}$,
the power being the $\mathbb{N}$-valued exponentiation of [[def-nat-power]].

Both degenerate cases are covered and neither is a stipulation. If
$B = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function $B \to A$, the empty function, so
$\lvert A^{\varnothing}\rvert = 1 = \lvert A\rvert^{0}$ **even when
$A = \varnothing$**. If $A = \varnothing$ and $B \ne \varnothing$ there is no
function at all, so $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = 0 = 0^{\lvert B\rvert}$ with
$\lvert B\rvert \ge 1$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$. By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot m$ ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), there is a unique function
$\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, written $n \mapsto m^{n}$, with

$$m^{0} = 1, \qquad m^{\sigma(n)} = m^{n} \cdot m \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Both the base and the value are natural numbers, so $m^n \in \mathbb{N}$ for all
$m, n$. In particular $m^{1} = m^{0}\cdot m = m$ and $m^{2} = m \cdot m$.

**Why a new item is needed.** [[def-integer-power]] defines $a^{n}$ for a
**real** base $a$, so its value is a real number. The counts on this page,
$\lvert A^{B}\rvert$ and $\lvert\mathcal{P}(A)\rvert$ among them, are natural
numbers, and an identity between them has to be an identity in $\mathbb{N}$. The
two operations are related by clause (d) below and by nothing weaker.

**(a) $0^{0} = 1$ and $0^{n} = 0$ for $n \ge 1$.** The first is the base clause.
For the second, $0^{\sigma(n)} = 0^{n}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause $x \cdot 0 = 0$
being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and every $n \ge 1$ is a
successor.

**(b) $1^{n} = 1$ for every $n$.** Induction: $1^{0} = 1$, and
$1^{\sigma(n)} = 1^{n}\cdot 1 = 1^{n}$ ([[lem-nat-mult-identity]],
[[thm-induction-principle]]).

**(c) $m^{p+q} = m^{p}\,m^{q}$ and $(m p)^{q} = m^{q} p^{q}$.** Both by induction
on $q$, using associativity and commutativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]). For the first, at
$q = 0$ we have $m^{p+0} = m^{p} = m^{p}\cdot 1 = m^{p}m^{0}$, and
$m^{p+\sigma(q)} = m^{\sigma(p+q)} = m^{p+q}\cdot m = (m^{p}m^{q})\cdot m = m^{p}\,m^{\sigma(q)}$,
using $p + \sigma(q) = \sigma(p+q)$ ([[def-nat-addition]]). For the second, at
$q = 0$ both sides are $1$, and
$(mp)^{\sigma(q)} = (mp)^{q}(mp) = m^{q}p^{q}mp = m^{\sigma(q)}p^{\sigma(q)}$.

**(d) The bridge into $\mathbb{R}$.** With $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$
the canonical natural ([[def-canonical-natural]]) and $x^{n}$ the integer power
of [[def-integer-power]],

$$\iota\big(m^{n}\big) = \iota(m)^{n} \qquad (m, n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Induction on $n$: at $n = 0$ both sides are $1$, since $\iota(1) = 1$; and
$\iota(m^{\sigma(n)}) = \iota(m^{n}\cdot m) = \iota(m^{n})\,\iota(m) = \iota(m)^{n}\iota(m) = \iota(m)^{\sigma(n)}$,
the second equality being the multiplicativity of $\iota$ (clause 0 of
[[lem-nat-finite-sum-laws-and-the-canonical-embedding]]) and the last the
recursion clause of [[def-integer-power]].

**(e) $m^{n}$ is a constant product.** $m^{n} = \prod_{k<n} m$, the
$\mathbb{N}$-valued product of the constant list
([[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]). Induction: at $n = 0$ both sides are $1$,
and $\prod_{k<\sigma(n)} m = \big(\prod_{k<n} m\big)\cdot m = m^{n}\cdot m = m^{\sigma(n)}$.

For all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$(x+y)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k<n+1} \iota\binom{n}{k}\, x^{k}\, y^{\,n-k},$$

where the powers are the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], the sum is the
real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] over $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$, the difference
$n-k$ is a genuine one because $k \le n$ throughout the range, and $\iota$ is the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]].

**The coefficient is $\iota\binom{n}{k}$ and not $\binom{n}{k}$.** A binomial
coefficient is a natural number, that is a von Neumann natural, that is a set; it
is not an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and it enters the field through $\iota$.

**The identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$ and only in $\mathbb{R}$.** The same
proof uses nothing but commutativity, associativity, distributivity and
natural-number multiples of a ring element, so a commutative-ring version is
available wherever rings are; rings are not available at this point in the
reading order, and the ring statement is a separate statement, to be made where
they are. See the Remarks below.

Let $a, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, let $c \in \mathbb{N}$, and let
$m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with $\sum^{\mathbb{N}}$ and $\prod^{\mathbb{N}}$ as in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]] and $\sum^{\mathbb{R}}$, $\prod^{\mathbb{R}}$
as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Let $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so $\iota(0) = 0$ and
$\iota(\sigma(n)) = \iota(n) + 1$. Then:

0. **$\iota$ is additive and multiplicative.** $\iota(1) = 1$, and
   $\iota(m+n) = \iota(m) + \iota(n)$ and $\iota(m n) = \iota(m)\,\iota(n)$ for
   **all** $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, the cases where a factor is $0$ included.
1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Constants.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} c = n \cdot c$, the summand being the constant list.
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ and $d := n - m$, then
   $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{j<d} a_{m+j}$, and
   $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{j<d} a_{m+j}\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for every $k < n$ then
   $\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$; and $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every $j < n$.
5. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$;
   and if $a_k \ne 0$ for every $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ne 0$.
6. **The bridge into $\mathbb{R}$.**
   $\displaystyle\iota\Big(\sum^{\mathbb{N}}_{k<n} a_k\Big) = \sum^{\mathbb{R}}_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
   and
   $\displaystyle\iota\Big(\prod^{\mathbb{N}}_{k<n} a_k\Big) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$.
7. **$\iota$ is strictly increasing, hence injective.** $m < n$ if and only if
   $\iota(m) < \iota(n)$, and $m = n$ if and only if $\iota(m) = \iota(n)$.

Clauses 6 and 7 together are the licence used everywhere below: an identity
between natural numbers may be proved by proving the corresponding identity
between their canonical naturals in $\mathbb{R}$, and conversely a real identity
whose two sides are canonical naturals is an identity in $\mathbb{N}$.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.

For all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$(x+y)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k<n+1} \iota\binom{n}{k}\, x^{k}\, y^{\,n-k},$$

where the powers are the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], the sum is the
real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] over $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$, the difference
$n-k$ is a genuine one because $k \le n$ throughout the range, and $\iota$ is the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]].

**The coefficient is $\iota\binom{n}{k}$ and not $\binom{n}{k}$.** A binomial
coefficient is a natural number, that is a von Neumann natural, that is a set; it
is not an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and it enters the field through $\iota$.

**The identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$ and only in $\mathbb{R}$.** The same
proof uses nothing but commutativity, associativity, distributivity and
natural-number multiples of a ring element, so a commutative-ring version is
available wherever rings are; rings are not available at this point in the
reading order, and the ring statement is a separate statement, to be made where
they are. See the Remarks below.

For $x>0$, define the **integral logarithm**

$$L(x):=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t},$$

using the oriented integral when $x<1$
([[def-oriented-integral]]).

This is well defined. The function $t\mapsto1/t$ is continuous wherever
$t\neq0$ by the quotient clause of
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. For $x\neq1$ it is therefore continuous on the nondegenerate compact interval
with endpoints $1$ and $x$, hence Riemann integrable there by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], whose hypothesis is $a<b$. At $x=1$ the
interval is degenerate and that theorem does not apply; there
[[def-oriented-integral]] stipulates $\int_1^1f=0$, so $L(1)=0$ directly.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

For every $x>0$,

$$L'(x)=\frac1x,$$

and $L(1)=0$.

For all $x,y>0$,

$$L(xy)=L(x)+L(y).$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.
The function $L:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing.

For $x>0$,

$$L(1/x)=-L(x).$$

For every integer $m$,

$$L(x^m)=mL(x),$$

and in particular $L(2^m)=mL(2)$. Moreover, $L(2)>0$.

For every $x>0$,

$$L(x)=\log x.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The map $\iota(n) = [(n,0)]$ is injective and preserves addition,
multiplication, and order. Its image is exactly the set of nonnegative
integers, so every $x \ge 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ is $\iota(k)$ for a unique
natural $k$.
For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $m < n \iff \sigma(m) \le n$ ([[def-nat-order]]). Consequently there is no $k$ with $n < k < \sigma(n)$: the successor $\sigma(n)$ is the immediate successor of $n$.

The relation of [[def-int-order]] is well defined and is a total order on
$\mathbb{Z}$; it is compatible with addition ($x \le y$ implies
$x + z \le y + z$) and positives are closed under multiplication
($0 < x$ and $0 < y$ imply $0 < xy$). Thus $\mathbb{Z}$ is a totally
ordered commutative ring.

derivations.claim: Put $\mathcal W=[m]^k$ and fix a bijection from the finite initial segment of size $m^k$ onto $\mathcal W$, whose existence is [F2]. Scan that finite segment in its natural order, retaining a word exactly when its Hamming distance from every previously retained word is greater than $r$. The scan terminates; its retained set $\mathcal C$ has pairwise distances greater than $r$, and every word not retained lies in a radius-$r$ ball about an earlier retained word.

A Hamming ball of radius $r$ has cardinality $B=\sum_{j=0}^r\binom{k}{j}(m-1)^j$: choose the $j$ coordinates that differ and then one of the other $m-1$ symbols at each such coordinate; different values of $j$ give disjoint sets, so [F3] counts the union.

Regard natural quantities as their real images under $\iota_{\mathbb R}$ as fixed in [F2]. Since $m\ge2$ and $j\le r\le k/4$, $\log(\iota_{\mathbb R}(m)-1)\ge0$, and the natural-power bridge in [F2] and the integer-power identity in [F5] give $\iota_{\mathbb R}((m-1)^j)=\exp(\iota_{\mathbb R}(j)\log(\iota_{\mathbb R}(m)-1))\le\exp((\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)/4)\log(\iota_{\mathbb R}(m)-1))$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

For every $x>0$,

$$L'(x)=\frac1x,$$

and $L(1)=0$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For every $x>0$,

$$L(x)=\log x.$$

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $M\ge2$ be an integer, let $P_1,\ldots,P_M$ be probability measures on
one measurable sample space, and let $J$ be uniform on $[M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}$.
Conditional on $J=j$, let the observation $X$ have law $P_j$. Define the
mixture law
$$\bar P:=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M P_j$$
and the **mutual information** of this finite experiment by
$$I(J;X):=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M D(P_j\|\bar P).$$
The set function $\bar P$ is a probability measure: for disjoint measurable
sets $(A_m)$, countable additivity of the $P_j$ gives
$$\bar P\!\left(\bigcup_m A_m\right)=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_mP_j(A_m).$$
The finite sum commutes with the increasing partial-sum limits of these
nonnegative series, so
$$\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_mP_j(A_m)=\sum_m\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^MP_j(A_m)=\sum_m\bar P(A_m),$$
so $\bar P$ is countably additive; also $\bar P(\varnothing)=0$ and
$\bar P(X)=1$. Here $D$ is the directional KL
divergence of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], and logarithms are natural.
For every measurable $A$, $P_j(A)\le M\bar P(A)$, so $P_j\ll\bar P$. Let
$r_j=dP_j/d\bar P$ be a finite-valued nonnegative density representative
provided by [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. If
$\bar P(\{r_j>M\})>0$, then for some integer $q\ge1$ the set
$E_q:=\{r_j\ge M+1/q\}$ has positive $\bar P$-measure. The change-of-measure
identity [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]] would give
$$P_j(E_q)=\int_{E_q}r_j\,d\bar P\ge(M+1/q)\bar P(E_q)>M\bar P(E_q),$$
contradicting $P_j(E_q)\le M\bar P(E_q)$. Hence $r_j\le M$ almost everywhere.
The densities also satisfy $M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^M r_j=1$ $\bar P$-almost
everywhere: for each measurable $A$,
$$\bar P(A)=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^MP_j(A)=\int_A\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^Mr_j\,d\bar P,$$
so $M^{-1}\sum_jr_j$ and the constant function $1$ are both densities of
$\bar P$ with respect to itself. They agree almost everywhere by
[[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]].
For $0\le t\le M$, the positive part of $t\log t$ is at most $M\log M$,
while its negative part is bounded by $1/e$ in
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Thus every term in the finite sum is
well-defined and finite.

The uniform prior is part of this definition. A nonuniform prior requires its

of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and

[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],

parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$

is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

   $$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A),$$
   as given by [[cor-finite-complex-measures-admit-integrable-radon-nikodym-densities]].

In both cases the derivative is not a distinguished pointwise function: it is determined only up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality in the sense of [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]].

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For every $x>0$,

$$L'(x)=\frac1x,$$

and $L(1)=0$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of von Neumann naturals
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ is itself the set of its predecessors,
the order being the additive order of [[def-nat-order]] identified with
membership in [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists ([[def-equinumerous]],
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). A set $A$ is **finite** when
$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable]]).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

**(d) Equality of cardinalities is equinumerosity.** For finite $A$ and $B$:
$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

For $x>0$, define the **integral logarithm**

$$L(x):=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t},$$

using the oriented integral when $x<1$
([[def-oriented-integral]]).

This is well defined. The function $t\mapsto1/t$ is continuous wherever
$t\neq0$ by the quotient clause of
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. For $x\neq1$ it is therefore continuous on the nondegenerate compact interval
with endpoints $1$ and $x$, hence Riemann integrable there by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], whose hypothesis is $a<b$. At $x=1$ the
interval is degenerate and that theorem does not apply; there
[[def-oriented-integral]] stipulates $\int_1^1f=0$, so $L(1)=0$ directly.

For every $x>0$,

$$L(x)=\log x.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Since $\bar P\ge P_j/M$, each $P_j\ll\bar P$. Choose densities $p_j=dP_j/d\bar P$ and set $\pi_j=p_j/M$. Then $\sum_j\pi_j=1$ $\bar P$-almost everywhere and $0\le\pi_j\le1$ by [F1]. The mutual-information definition [F1] and KL formula [F2] give $I(J;X)=\int\sum_j\pi_j\log(M\pi_j)\,d\bar P=\log M-\int H(\pi(x))\,\bar P(dx).$ All terms are integrable because $u\log u$ is bounded on $[0,1]$ and the sum is finite.

Let $L$ be any randomized decision in $[M]$ based on $X$, with $q_l(x)=P(L=l\mid X=x)$ given by its probability kernel. Put $w_l=\int q_l\,d\bar P$. When $w_l>0$, the conditional probability vector of $J$ given $L=l$ has entries $\eta_{lj}=w_l^{-1}\int q_l(x)\pi_j(x)\,\bar P(dx)$. Apply Jensen to $u\mapsto u\log u$ for each coordinate under the probability measure $q_l\,d\bar P/w_l$, sum over $j$, and use $\sum_j\pi_j=\sum_j\eta_{lj}=1$. The result is $H(\eta_l)\ge w_l^{-1}\int q_l(x)H(\pi(x))\,\bar P(dx)$. Multiplication by $w_l$ and summation over positive $w_l$ yields $H(J\mid L):=\sum_lw_lH(\eta_l)\ge\int H(\pi(x))\,d\bar P$; zero-probability outputs contribute zero. Hence $\log M-H(J\mid L)\le I(J;X)$ by step 1.1.

If some $P_j\not\ll Q$, then $K_Q=+\infty$ and the bound is vacuous. Otherwise write $r_j=dP_j/dQ$. If the positive part of $r_j\log r_j$ has infinite integral, then $D(P_j\|Q)=+\infty$; if it is finite, the negative part is finite by [F2] and Jensen [F3] for the convex function $u\log u$ gives $D(P_j\|Q)=\int r_j\log r_j\,dQ\ge0$. Thus every divergence is nonnegative; therefore $K_Q<\infty$ implies that every term is finite. Set $\bar r=M^{-1}\sum_jr_j=d\bar P/dQ$. On $\{\bar r>0\}$, $r_j=M\bar r\pi_j$ $Q$-almost everywhere: by [F2], for every measurable $A$, $P_j(A)=\int_Ap_j\,d\bar P=\int_Ap_j\bar r\,dQ$, where $p_j=dP_j/d\bar P=M\pi_j$ from step 1.1; uniqueness of the density gives the identity. Hence $r_j\log(r_j/\bar r)=\bar r\,\psi(M\pi_j)$. This is integrable: $M\pi_j\in[0,M]$, $|u\log u|\le1/e$ for $0\le u\le1$ by [F2], and $0\le u\log u\le M\log M$ for $1\le u\le M$ by monotonicity in [F3], while $\bar r$ has integral one. The identity $r_j\log r_j=r_j\log(r_j/\bar r)+r_j\log\bar r$ holds on $\{\bar r>0\}$; on $\{\bar r=0\}$ all $r_j=0$ and every term is set to zero. Jensen and [F3] give $\bar r\log\bar r\le M^{-1}\sum_jr_j\log r_j$, so its positive part is integrable; its negative part is bounded by [F2]. Integrating the identity and averaging therefore gives $K_Q=I(J;X)+D(\bar P\|Q).$ Finally Jensen under the probability law $Q$ yields $D(\bar P\|Q)=\int\bar r\log\bar r\,dQ\ge(\int\bar r\,dQ)\log(\int\bar r\,dQ)=0$. Therefore $I(J;X)\le K_Q$.

For the error event $E=\{L\ne J\}$, $E$ is determined by $(J,L)$, so $H(E,J\mid L)=H(J\mid L)$. Expanding the finite conditional entropy sums and factoring $P(E=e,J=j\mid L=l)=P(E=e\mid L=l)P(J=j\mid E=e,L=l)$ gives $H(J\mid L)=H(E\mid L)+H(J\mid E,L).$ For each conditional law, entropy on at most $N$ points is at most $\log N$: if its probabilities are $s_1,\ldots,s_N$, Jensen for $u\log u$ gives $N^{-1}\sum_r(Ns_r)\log(Ns_r)\ge0$, which rearranges to $-\sum_rs_r\log s_r\le\log N$. Thus $H(E\mid L)\le\log2$; when $E=0$, $J=L$ has entropy zero, and when $E=1$, at most $M-1$ indices remain, so $H(J\mid E,L)\le P(E=1)\log(M-1)\le P(E=1)\log M$. Combining this with step 2.1 and $I(J;X)\le K_Q$ from step 2.2 proves $P(L\ne J)\ge1-\frac{K_Q+\log2}{\log M}$ when $K_Q<\infty$; for $K_Q=\infty$ the bound is vacuous.

Given an estimator action $A\in\mathcal T$, choose $L$ to be the smallest index minimizing $\rho(A,t_l)$. This is a measurable finite-valued decision because each distance to a fixed target is continuous and ties are resolved by the fixed index order; composing the map with the estimator kernel gives the randomized decision kernel of step 2.1 by [F5]. If $L\ne J=j$, nearest choice and the triangle inequality give $\Delta\le\rho(t_j,t_L)\le\rho(t_j,A)+\rho(A,t_L)\le2\rho(A,t_j)$, so squared loss is at least $\Delta^2/4$ on the error event. Step 3.1 therefore gives the average risk bound. The maximum risk is at least its uniform average; taking the infimum over procedures using [F6] and [F7] gives the minimax conclusion.

citations.quote: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra

probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.

parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The

$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable

Let $d,k$ be natural numbers with $1\le k\le d/2$. Let $m$ and $r$ be the
natural quotients determined by
$$mk\le d<(m+1)k,\qquad 4r\le k<4(r+1).$$
Thus $m\ge2$. Write $[m]=\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ and give $[m]^k$ the Hamming
distance $d_H(\omega,\omega')=\#\{j<k:\omega_j\ne\omega'_j\}$. There is a
set $\mathcal C\subseteq[m]^k$ such that distinct $\omega,\omega'\in\mathcal C$
satisfy $d_H(\omega,\omega')>r$ and
$$\log|\mathcal C|\ge \frac{k}{1024}\log\!\left(\frac{ed}{k}\right).$$
For each $\omega\in\mathcal C$, place one $1$ in each of the first $k$ disjoint
coordinate blocks of size $m$, at position $\omega_j$ in block $j$, and put
$0$ in all remaining coordinates of $\mathbb R^d$. The resulting vectors
$u^\omega\in\{0,1\}^d$ have exactly $k$ nonzero coordinates and satisfy
$$\|u^\omega-u^{\omega'}\|_2^2>k/2\qquad(\omega\ne\omega').$$

$$K_Q:=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M D(P_j\|Q)\in[0,+\infty].$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, define the **integral logarithm**

$$L(x):=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t},$$

using the oriented integral when $x<1$
([[def-oriented-integral]]).

This is well defined. The function $t\mapsto1/t$ is continuous wherever
$t\neq0$ by the quotient clause of
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. For $x\neq1$ it is therefore continuous on the nondegenerate compact interval
with endpoints $1$ and $x$, hence Riemann integrable there by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], whose hypothesis is $a<b$. At $x=1$ the
interval is degenerate and that theorem does not apply; there
[[def-oriented-integral]] stipulates $\int_1^1f=0$, so $L(1)=0$ directly.

For every $x>0$,

$$L(x)=\log x.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], choose a code $\mathcal C$ of size $M$ with associated $u^\omega\in\{0,1\}^d$, each having exactly $k$ ones and pairwise squared distance greater than $k/2$. Its logarithmic size is positive because $ed/k\ge2e>1$ by [F8], so $M\ge2$.

Suppose $M=2$. The size bound in [F2] implies $k\log(ed/k)\le1024\log2<1024$ by [F8]. The two means $\mu^0=0$ and $\mu^1=b e_1$, where $b=\sigma/(2\sqrt n)$, both belong to $\Theta_{k,d}$ because $k\ge1$. Let $\pi_1:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be first-coordinate projection and define the scalar action kernel $K_1(y,B):=K(y,\pi_1^{-1}(B))$ for every Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R$. Since $\pi_1$ is Borel, each $K_1(y,\cdot)$ is the pushforward probability under $\pi_1$ and $y\mapsto K_1(y,B)$ is measurable, so [F5] applies to $K_1$. For $j=0,1$, define $R^{(1)}_j(K_1):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R}(x-\mu^j_1)^2K_1(y,dx)P_{\mu^j}(dy)$. The pushforward integral identity here follows from the definition of $K_1$ for indicators and then for nonnegative functions by simple approximation; together with $\|z-\mu^j\|_2^2\ge(z_1-\mu^j_1)^2$, it gives $R_{\mu^j}(K)\ge R^{(1)}_j(K_1)$. The scalar target gap is $b$. The KL divergence of the two full observation laws is $nb^2/(2\sigma^2)=1/8$ by [F3], so [F6] gives $\|P_{\mu^0}-P_{\mu^1}\|_{\rm TV}\le1/4$. Applying [F5] to the scalar kernel and these two laws yields $\max_jR^{(1)}_j(K_1)\ge b^2(1-1/4)/8=3b^2/32=3\sigma^2/(128n)$, and therefore $\max_jR_{\mu^j}(K)\ge3\sigma^2/(128n)$. Since $1024/200000<3/128$, this exceeds $\sigma^2 k\log(ed/k)/(200000n)$.
Suppose $M\ge3$. Put $a^2=\sigma^2\log M/(4nk)$ and $\mu^\omega=a u^\omega$. These means belong to $\Theta_{k,d}$, and their pairwise squared distances exceed $a^2k/2$ by step 1.1.

Take $Q=P_0$, the zero-mean Gaussian law. By [F3], for every $\omega\in\mathcal C$, $D(P_{\mu^\omega}\|P_0)=\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}\|a u^\omega\|_2^2=\frac{na^2k}{2\sigma^2}=\frac{\log M}{8}.$ Thus the average reference divergence equals $\log M/8$.

Since $M\ge3$, $\log2/\log M\le\log2/\log3<2/3$: the strict inequality follows from $3\log2=\log8<\log9=2\log3$, using $8<9$, monotonicity, and the product law in [F8]. Thus $1-((\log M)/8+\log2)/\log M\ge7/8-2/3=5/24>1/5$. Apply [F4] with separation $\Delta=a\sqrt{k/2}$ and reference $P_0$. Every estimator's average risk on the code is at least $\frac{\Delta^2}{4}\cdot\frac15=\frac{a^2k}{40}=\frac{\sigma^2\log M}{160n}\ge\frac{\sigma^2 k\log(ed/k)}{163840n}.$ The supremum over $\Theta_{k,d}$ dominates this finite-code average.

In the $M\ge3$ case, $1/163840>1/200000$, so step 4.1 implies the claimed bound. In the $M=2$ case it follows from step 2.1. For every estimator, the supremum risk over $\Theta_{k,d}$ is at least the finite submodel average or two-point maximum just proved; taking the infimum over estimators in the defined minimax value preserves the bound.

such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

Assume AC and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau>0$. For the normal location
laws with common variance $\tau^2$,
$$D\bigl(N(a,\tau^2)\|N(b,\tau^2)\bigr)=\frac{(a-b)^2}{2\tau^2}.$$

Assume AC. Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$. For each $i<n$, let
$(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ be a measurable space and let $P_i,Q_i$ be probability
measures on it. On the finite product measurable space set
$$P=\bigotimes_{i<n}P_i,\qquad Q=\bigotimes_{i<n}Q_i.$$
With the KL convention of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]],
$$D(P\|Q)=\sum_{i<n}D(P_i\|Q_i),$$
where a sum with an infinite term is $+\infty$.

Assume AC. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one measurable space, with
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|,$$
the event-supremum convention without a factor $1/2$,
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}\le\sqrt{\frac12D(P\|Q)}.$$
If $P\not\ll Q$, the right side is $+\infty$ by the definition of KL
divergence.

Let $d\ge1$, $a>0$, and consider the finite experiment indexed by
$\omega\in\{0,1\}^d$ with sample laws $P_\omega$. The target is
$t_\omega=a\omega\in\mathbb R^d$, the action is in $\mathbb R^d$, and loss
is squared Euclidean distance. For each coordinate $i$, let $\omega^{(i)}$
denote the vector with bit $i$ flipped, and set
$$v:=\max_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d,\ 1\le i\le d} \|P_\omega-P_{\omega^{(i)}}\|_{\rm TV}.$$
For every randomized estimator kernel $K$,
$$\max_{\omega}R_\omega(K)\ge\frac{a^2d}{8}(1-v),$$
and the same lower bound holds for the minimax risk. The total variation
convention is $\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.
